extracted.intended_audience: telescopic planetary observers / astronomers (e.g., observatory observers of Mars)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and observational criteria for detecting, measuring, mapping, and establishing the reality of the straight 'canals' on Mars, and for rejecting optical/illusory explanations. Covers perceptual thresholds, measurement methods, network statistics, and tests of alternative hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canals are geometric straight lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The markings are lines in the precise geometric sense and are furthermore straight lines — "they look to have been laid down by rule and compass." Ninety per cent are absolutely straight; the remainder curve symmetrically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This straightness is a primary diagnostic: unlike natural terrestrial features, the canals show an unnatural regularity of look. Use repeated careful observations to judge absolute directness throughout a feature's course; straightness distinguishes canals from rivers, ordinary markings, cracks, and other natural analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite direction and absolute directness
rubrics_metrics.description: Canals show definiteness of direction: they run straight throughout their course and show great-circle directness between endpoints — many canals swerve neither right nor left of the great circle joining their termini.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess directness by following a canal's path over its entire visible extent; unexpected deviations argue against canal identification. Great-circle alignment over thousands of miles is a key feature: check for consistent direction across oppositions and observing sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform width (telegraphic slenderness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each line maintains a uniform width from beginning to end; apparent breadth is minimal — more a function of being seen than measurable breadth ('the width, too, is telegraphic').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate width by comparison experiments (e.g., projecting a known-diameter wire against the sky or using a micrometer thread). Account for atmospheric/instrumental/personal broadening; improved conditions produce 'emaceration' (lines appear finer). Typical perceptible lower-limit widths estimated ~1 mile (practical limit ~2 miles); larger canals commonly 15–20 miles; the largest (Nilosyrtis) estimated 25–30 miles.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-dimensional character vs two-dimensional main markings
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental dark/bright markings have two-dimensional extension; the canals are essentially one-dimensional (long narrow filaments) and are intrinsically distinct from the main markings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use morphological comparison: canals appear as linear filaments with little measurable breadth, whereas the main albedo features are extended regions. This distinction supports treating canals as a separate class of phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detectability thresholds and retinal summation
rubrics_metrics.description: A canal's visibility depends on its length and the summation of small retinal stimuli along that length; a wire subtending ~0.69 seconds of arc is a practical threshold above which an external stimulus can be distinguished from purely retinal effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use threshold experiments (wire at known distance subtending arcseconds) to discriminate true markings from retinal/optic artefacts. If a marking produces an impression significantly above the 0.69'' threshold and is repeatable, it is unlikely to be self-deception. Below ~0.59'' the stimulus is too weak to be seen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic interdependence and junction structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Canals are interdependent: they meet at terminals in junctions of many lines (3–14 lines at a node), forming a planet-covering network of polygons (areolas) that tessellates the surface like a geodetic survey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map and collate multiple observations to reveal the network. Expect junction-rich topology (not isolated random lines); increasing resolution will subdivide polygons but preserve clean-cut sides. The communal pattern is diagnostic of non-random, law-governed origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-random placement (statistical/planet-wide coherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The canals are not fortuitously placed; their arrangement is planet-wide and linked across large areas, transcending local zonal differences. Distribution is fairly even across longitudes and latitudes (except poleward crowding), indicating a cause operating globally rather than locally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform zonal counts and compute canal-lengths per latitudinal band (example table provided). Compare opposite-season maps to annul seasonal effects. Look for planet-wide mesh and increased canal density toward poles; such distributions argue against purely local physical causes (e.g., cracks or rivers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to topography and relative (post-formation) timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Canals tend to emanate from salient points of the main albedo features (indentations, bays, dark radiants) and align with obvious topographic features; this suggests canals were superposed on the pre-existing main markings (i.e., formed later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference canal terminations and origins with maps of the main markings. If canals systematically connect the most suggestive points for intercommunication, interpret this as evidence of post-formation superposition rather than coeval origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and unbroken character (not cracks or riverbeds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Canals remain unbroken and maintain uniform size throughout great distances; they do not show the typical discontinuity, branching, or irregular outlines expected of cracks, rivers, or contraction features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuity and uniformity as tests: long, straight, unbroken courses with uniform width over thousands of miles are inconsistent with known crack/rift or drainage processes. Compare lunar rills and terrestrial fissures for contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemination (double canals) — properties and reality tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemination: certain canals appear as twin parallel lines, equidistant throughout their course, of the same size and length. Pairs may replace previously single lines and are often revealed suddenly under steady seeing conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require steady atmospheric definition and repeated confirmation; measure inter-line spacing (each canal shows a characteristic mean width). Gemination is canal-specific (some canals always double, others always single) and repeatable under comparable conditions — these properties are evidence for objectivity rather than optical artefact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refutation criteria for the diplopic (out-of-focus) hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed properties contradict diplopia: (1) focus is a reflex and observers detect out-of-focus states, (2) doubles appear unpredictably (flashes) and cannot be focused on, (3) measured separation for a given canal is constant over epochs, (4) diplopia would affect all similarly-inclined objects uniformly but gemination is canal-specific, (5) mean widths differ between canals whereas diplopic mean would be common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five empirical tests when evaluating whether a doubled appearance could be produced by diplopia. Repeat observations across sessions and observers to check consistency of separations and selectivity of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refutation criteria for interference/optical diffraction hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference/diffraction explanations predict (1) a bright central streak/backbone, (2) a fixed separation determined by aperture, and (3) aperture-dependence of separation — none of which match observations (no backbone seen; width not a function of aperture; idiosyncratic canal widths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary telescope aperture and compare measured separations; check for predicted fringe patterns. If separations and presence/absence of doubles are independent of aperture and no bright backbone is present, interference is not a viable explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refutation criteria for illusion/psychological-copying hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple illusion arguments (e.g., observers or copyists inventing lines) fail because illusory lines arise only at the limit of vision and the well-seen canals are well within visibility; experienced observers have a 'peculiar sense of reality' enabling them to distinguish true from false markings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between limit-of-vision syntheses and repeatable, vivid sightings within clear seeing conditions. Use repeated, independent observations (including photographic attempts where feasible) and contrast novice misperceptions (e.g., schoolboy drawing experiments) with expert repeatability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation practice, mapping, and measurement methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliable canal detection requires trained observers, steady seeing, collating observations across sessions/oppositions, and measurement by comparison with known standards (telegraph wire experiments, micrometer threads). Maps from single oppositions are informative but blending many oppositions yields a more uniform and complete distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train observers to recognize true vs. false impressions; use controlled experiments to determine perceptual thresholds; project/photograph for corroboration; synthesize maps from multiple oppositions to reduce seasonal/seeing biases and to reveal the underlying mesh.
